observation_summary: The MathUtils.factorialDouble(n) method produces incorrect results for n >= 17 due to precision issues, likely caused by an underlying implementation that uses logarithms or floating-point arithmetic instead of direct integer multiplication.
hypothesis: The implementation of factorialDouble(n) uses an algorithm (likely involving logarithms or floating-point approximations) that loses precision for larger inputs, whereas a direct iterative multiplication approach would maintain the required precision for long-based factorials.
prediction: The code for MathUtils.factorialDouble(n) will show a computational strategy that performs floating-point operations (like Math.exp(Math.log(...))) instead of a simple loop multiplying integers.
experiment_rationale: The bug report explicitly suggests replacing the current implementation with a simple loop or precomputed array to avoid rounding errors, confirming the issue is the chosen computational strategy.
reasoning_summary: The defect is a classic case of an incorrect computational strategy (Algorithm/Method). The procedure used to calculate the factorial is mathematically sound for small numbers but fails for larger ones due to precision loss inherent in the chosen algorithm. It is not a missing check (Checking), a wrong constant (Assignment/Initialization), or a design-level capability gap (Function/Class/Object).
evidence_used: Bug report description: 'The result of MathUtils.factorial( n ) for n = 17, 18, 19 is wrong, probably because of rounding errors in the double calculations.'
Bug report description: 'I suggest implementing a simple loop to multiply the long result - or even using a precomputed long[] - instead of adding logarithms.'

alternative_types.why_not_primary: The issue is not a single wrong value or initialization, but the entire computational procedure used to derive the result.
The capability (factorial calculation) exists; it is just implemented with an algorithm that is insufficiently precise for the required range.
